title: Optimal approximation for nonmonotone submodular maximization over a matroid
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
formal:
Determine the optimal expected approximation ratio for maximizing a nonnegative, not necessarily monotone submodular set function subject to one matroid independence constraint, in the polynomial-time oracle model specified below.

For an instance \(J=(n,f,\mathcal I)\), write
\[
\operatorname{OPT}(J)=\max\{f(S):S\in\mathcal I\}.
\]
Let \(\mathscr A\) be the class of uniform randomized oracle algorithms defined below: each always outputs an independent set and has a polynomial bound on its total number of elementary operations, on every valid instance and every random tape. Define
\[
\mathcal R=\left\{\alpha\in[0,1]:
 \exists A\in\mathscr A\ \forall J\
 \mathbb E_{\omega}\!\left[f\!\left(A^{f,\mathcal I}(n;\omega)\right)\right]
 \ge \alpha\,\operatorname{OPT}(J)\right\},
\qquad
\rho_{\mathrm{mat}}=\sup\mathcal R.
\]
The universal quantifier ranges over every finite ground-set size, every nonnegative submodular function on that ground set, and every matroid on it. The approximation constant and algorithm are chosen before the instance. The target is the real number \(\rho_{\mathrm{mat}}\); it is not assumed that an algorithm attains the supremum. Supply a real answer \(a\) with a Lean-checked proof that
\[
|a-\rho_{\mathrm{mat}}|\le \frac{1}{100}.
\]

why: This is a central approximation question for a general combinatorial optimization model, rather than a guarantee for one application or a running-time refinement. Matroids include cardinality, partition and linear-independence constraints, and submodularity encompasses many cut, coverage and information objectives. Determining the optimal guarantee would identify the inherent cost of combining diminishing returns, potentially harmful additions and independence constraints. Unlike several neighboring monotone or unconstrained models, the known algorithmic and information-theoretic bounds still leave a substantial gap.
status_note: Open in the 2022 source, with a bounded later-source review through 16 September 2026. The checked discrete matroid approximation improved to 0.401 in Buchbinder–Feldman (preprint 2023; STOC 2024), while the checked oracle barrier remains 0.478. Chen and coauthors' March 2026 preprint explicitly describes the remaining gap as open. The September 2026 online continuous result does not claim optimality and is a different model. No verified resolution or interval meeting the card's 1/100 answer tolerance was found. The review inspected model definitions, theorem statements and limited supporting arguments; it is not an exhaustive literature review, a full proof audit or a Lean verification.

progress.text: Oveis Gharan and Vondrák prove that a \(0.478\) approximation under a matroid independence constraint would require exponentially many value queries.

Qi's ISAAC paper explicitly asks for the best achievable approximation for general matroid-constrained submodular maximization and proves \(0.478\) oracle hardness already under a cardinality constraint.
Buchbinder and Feldman's preprint gives the \(0.401\) guarantee; the work subsequently appears at STOC 2024.
The second revision of Chen and coauthors' preprint improves a deterministic approximation while explicitly retaining the general \(0.401\)-versus-\(0.478\) gap.

Recovered the background CSM target, specified its exact oracle and computation conventions, updated the known bounds, and defined numerical Lean acceptance without requiring attainment of the optimal ratio.

importance.reason: Individual assessment: the optimal approximation for nonnegative submodular maximization under one arbitrary matroid is a central structural question in approximation algorithms, unifying many independence-constrained objectives. It asks for the frontier of an entire oracle model, with implications extending beyond a single algorithm or application. The score reflects that breadth and the unresolved algorithm-versus-information gap, and replaces the explicitly unassessed midpoint 50.

sentences: The input is a nonnegative submodular set function and one matroid, accessed through exact value and independence oracles.
The goal is to choose an independent set with a large objective value, even though adding elements can reduce that value.
The target is the supremum of expected approximation factors achievable by a uniform randomized algorithm using polynomially many total oracle-model operations.
The checked literature gives a 0.401 approximation and a 0.478 value-query barrier, with the general gap explicitly retained in a March 2026 source.
A benchmark answer must determine that optimal real ratio within 1/100 and prove the claimed accuracy in Lean without assuming that the supremum is attained.

definitions:
For \(n\in\mathbb N_{0}\), the ground set is \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\), and \(2^{[n]}\) denotes its power set. The objective is a function \(f:2^{[n]}\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) satisfying
\[
f(S)+f(T)\ge f(S\cup T)+f(S\cap T)
\quad\text{for all }S,T\subseteq[n].
\]
This is submodularity. Monotonicity would additionally require \(f(S)\le f(T)\) whenever \(S\subseteq T\); no such requirement is imposed. Nonnegativity applies to every subset, including infeasible ones. No normalization \(f(\varnothing)=0\) is required.

A matroid independence family \(\mathcal I\subseteq2^{[n]}\) satisfies three axioms: \(\varnothing\in\mathcal I\); every subset of an element of \(\mathcal I\) belongs to \(\mathcal I\); and if \(S,T\in\mathcal I\) with \(|S|<|T|\), then some \(t\in T\setminus S\) satisfies \(S\cup\{t\}\in\mathcal I\). An output is any set in \(\mathcal I\), and need not be maximal. The rank, defined as \(\max_{S\in\mathcal I}|S|\), is unrestricted. A cardinality constraint is the special case \(\mathcal I=\{S:|S|\le k\}\).

The input explicitly supplies the integer \(n\) in binary, with zero represented by the single bit zero. Sets supplied to or returned by an oracle are represented by their \(n\)-bit incidence vectors. Two exact oracles are available: a value oracle returns the real number \(f(S)\), and an independence oracle returns the bit indicating whether \(S\in\mathcal I\). The oracles remain fixed throughout a run. Neither the full table of \(f\) nor a list of all independent sets is supplied, and there is no oracle for a continuous extension, its derivatives, or an optimum.

Fix the following exact-real oracle computation convention. An algorithm is one finite program with finite control, finitely many ordinary bit tapes and finitely many tapes of exact real cells. It may contain finitely many rational constants, each specified by a signed integer numerator and a positive integer denominator. Initially work tapes are blank or zero. Elementary instructions are ordinary bit-tape read/write and one-cell head moves; one-cell real-tape head moves; copying or loading a real cell; addition, subtraction, multiplication or division of a fixed finite number of currently addressed real cells; exact comparison of two such cells; obtaining one independent fair random bit; or one of the two oracle calls. Each instruction costs one operation. Division must have a nonzero divisor on every valid run. The query incidence vector must already have been written on the query tape; reading and writing its bits are charged by the bit-tape instructions. An oracle answer is deposited in a designated real cell or bit cell in one operation. Outputting the final incidence vector is also charged. Real cells have no instruction for inspecting a binary expansion or converting an arbitrary real directly into an integer.

This is a unit-cost exact-arithmetic oracle model: the size parameter is \(n\), and real answers are not charged by a bit length. All computation between queries is counted. Programs have no advice depending on \(n\) or the instance, no arbitrary real constants, and no other oracles. This explicit convention completes the source's polynomial-time/value-oracle formulation; it does not assert equivalence to a bit-complexity model for rational objectives.

Formally, \(A\in\mathscr A\) means that there are integers \(C\ge1\) and \(q\ge0\), fixed for that program, such that for every valid \(J=(n,f,\mathcal I)\) and every random tape \(\omega\), the program makes only valid operations and queries, halts within \(C(n+1)^q\) elementary operations, and outputs an \(n\)-bit vector encoding a member of \(\mathcal I\). Thus both its number of oracle queries and its other work are polynomially bounded. No feasibility error is allowed. The expectation in the guarantee concerns objective value, not feasibility or running time.

The random tape consists of independent fair bits, so each specified prefix of length \(r\) has probability \(2^{-r}\). For a program with the above clock, at most \(C(n+1)^q\) bits are read; its expected value is consequently a finite average over that many fair bits, with unused bits ignored. If \(\operatorname{OPT}(J)=0\), the multiplicative guarantee is automatically satisfied; no quotient by zero is used. Always returning the empty set guarantees factor zero, so \(\mathcal R\) is nonempty and its supremum is well-defined in \([0,1]\).
answer_criterion:
Supply a specified real number \(a\), or an unambiguous expression defining it, and a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of
\[
|a-\rho_{\mathrm{mat}}|\le \frac{1}{100}
\]
for exactly the instance class and algorithm class above. Merely restating the supremum that defines \(\rho_{\mathrm{mat}}\) is not a determination.

A certified interval is sufficient: give \(l,u\in[0,1]\), prove
\[
l\le\rho_{\mathrm{mat}}\le u,\qquad u-l\le\frac{1}{50},
\]
and use \(a=(l+u)/2\). To make explicit what both sides mean, the lower bound can be certified by proving
\[
\forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists A\in\mathscr A\
\forall J\
\mathbb E_{\omega}[f(A^{f,\mathcal I}(n;\omega))]
\ge(l-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(J).
\]
The upper bound can be certified by proving
\[
\forall\varepsilon>0\ \forall A\in\mathscr A\
\exists J\
\mathbb E_{\omega}[f(A^{f,\mathcal I}(n;\omega))]
<(u+\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(J).
\]
Membership in \(\mathscr A\) includes the full program, uniform polynomial clock and unconditional feasibility requirements from the definitions. In the lower statement the program and its polynomial constants may depend on \(\varepsilon\), but not on \(J\); the upper statement ranges over every such program and all possible polynomial degrees. This permits approaching a supremum without attaining it.

Exact determination is welcome but is not mandatory. A guarantee for a subclass of matroids or objectives, for deterministic algorithms alone, or for polynomially many queries with unrestricted computation does not by itself determine this target. Nor does an upper bound assuming an unproved complexity separation constitute the unconditional upper certificate above.

context_blocks.text: Qi's original question concerns general constrained submodular maximization: a single nonnegative submodular objective over independent sets of one matroid. Although the paper mainly studies a sum with a linear function, that linear term is absent from the extracted open question. The source measures approximation in expectation and running time polynomially in ground-set size.

The 2022 source records a \(0.385\) approximation and a \(0.478\) oracle inapproximability threshold. Qi also proves the latter threshold already for the cardinality-constrained special case. The upper bound therefore applies to algorithms for all matroids, but does not make the special case and general case identical problems.

Buchbinder and Feldman's STOC 2024 result improves the approximation guarantee to \(0.401\) for a matroid constraint. Their Corollary 1.3 is stated directly for the discrete set-function problem; the result is not merely a guarantee for a continuous objective with stronger oracle access.

The checked results give the conservative bracket \(401/1000\le\rho_{\mathrm{mat}}\le239/500\). Its width is \(77/1000\), larger than the benchmark's sufficient interval width \(1/50\). These bounds therefore do not already meet this card's numerical acceptance criterion.

A March 2026 preprint explicitly describes the remaining \(0.401\)-versus-\(0.478\) gap as open while improving a deterministic guarantee to \(0.385-\varepsilon\). A September 2026 online continuous-optimization preprint explicitly says its \(0.401\) result does not claim optimality. Neither supplies the requested determination in this card's offline randomized model.

Read the actual 16-page ISAAC 2022 proceedings PDF, especially p. 41:2: CSM returns an independent set of a given matroid and asks a polynomial-time-in-n expected multiplicative approximation. Its general optimal ratio remains open between the then-known 0.385 and 0.478 bounds. The very next paragraph turns to f+ell, which is the main paper topic but is not the extracted open question. Section 2 pp. 41:5–41:6 defines f as nonnegative on all subsets, gives the submodular inequality, uses value oracles and a matroid independent-set family. It does not impose f(empty)=0.

The source does not prescribe machine instructions, numeric bit encodings, a random-tape distribution or how the matroid is accessed at the bit level. The draft explicitly completes these with exact-real arithmetic, a membership oracle for independence, binary set queries, independent fair random bits, finite rational program constants and total polynomial operation cost. This is an editorial formalization of the polynomial-time oracle question, not an assertion that the paper itself fixes these instructions or that rational bit complexity and real-unit-cost complexity are equivalent.

The exact-real model counts both oracle calls and all intervening work, so it does not silently weaken polynomial time to polynomial query count with unlimited computation. Matroid rank is unrestricted, feasible output is required on every random tape, and the polynomial clock is uniform over objectives and matroids. Because the ratio is a supremum, arbitrarily close guarantees may use distinct finite programs and polynomial degrees; no algorithm attaining the endpoint is demanded.

Read the actual expanded Algorithmica publisher PDF, online 13 November 2023, volume year 2024, pp. 1080–1134. The old open gap remains in its introduction pp. 1081–1082. Theorem 4.1 on p. 1091 gives 0.478 inapproximability already for cardinality constraints, and Lemma 4.4 on the same page explicitly includes randomized algorithms in the value-query lower bound. This stronger special-case obstruction applies to the all-matroid algorithm class, but does not prove that cardinality and matroid optima coincide. The old arXiv:2205.15874 landing page displays only v1 dated 31 May 2022, so it is not the edition used for the journal pagination.

Read the author-hosted extended Oveis Gharan–Vondrak PDF associated with SODA 2011, abstract, introductory table and Theorem 5.4 (cached PDF p. 15). Its 0.478 result is for matroid independent sets; a separate 0.394 result concerns bases and must not be applied to this card. The complete hardness proof was not independently audited. The direct later Qi theorem supplies an additional checked primary statement of the same obstruction under the cardinality special case.

Read Buchbinder–Feldman arXiv:2311.01129v1, 2 November 2023, Theorem 1.2 and Corollary 1.3 p. 3. The latter directly states a polynomial-time 0.401 approximation for nonnegative submodular set functions under a matroid constraint. Appendix A pp. 38–39 explains access through the discrete value oracle, sampling error and the strict numerical slack beyond 0.401; this is not merely an exact-gradient-oracle theorem. Section 6 p. 31 still identifies a gap to 0.478, and also notes a tiny fourth-decimal improvement, so the card calls [0.401,0.478] a conservative bracket rather than claiming those decimals are exact frontier endpoints. Checked STOC 2024 metadata, pp. 1820–1831 and DOI 10.1145/3618260.3649630, against author and institutional publication pages; the cached full text is the arXiv edition.

Read Chen–Gao–Lin–Sun–Zhang arXiv:2603.11996v2, submitted 16 March 2026, abstract and Introduction pp. 1–3. The source explicitly calls the 0.401-versus-0.478 gap a remaining open challenge. Its advance is deterministic 0.385-epsilon, and therefore does not supersede the randomized lower guarantee in this card. The PDF typeset date is 17 March 2026, but the arXiv revision date is 16 March.

Read Aggarwal–Lu arXiv:2609.02145v1, submitted 2 September 2026, abstract and Introduction pp. 1–2. It matches the constructive 0.401 factor in an online continuous DR-submodular model and explicitly disclaims claiming optimality. Its online feedback, continuous objective and convex-feasibility assumptions are different from this card's discrete offline value/independence-oracle model. No theorem from that paper is used to alter the target or to establish a new discrete lower bound.

Bounded later searches through 16 September 2026 included general nonmonotone submodular matroid approximation, 0.401, 0.478, 2025/2026 and post-August-2026 queries. Surfaced deterministic, dynamic, streaming, symmetric, curvature-restricted and online results were distinguished from the general target. No matching ratio or sufficiently narrow two-sided interval was found. The current conservative interval has width 77/1000, exceeding 1/50, so the default numerical benchmark tolerance does not already render the card solved.

The Lean criterion uses a real answer with absolute error at most 1/100. Optional lower and upper certificates quantify over every valid input and every admissible algorithm, respectively; their epsilon quantifiers accommodate a nonattained supremum. The upper certificate is unconditional in the chosen oracle model. Results restricted to a family of algorithms, conditional complexity assumptions or stronger oracle access are not silently accepted as full upper bounds.
